result.summary: Latona, worn out and thirsty while carrying her twin children, is refused water by Lycian countrymen, who also muddy the pool. She curses them to live in the pool forever and they become frogs. A villager tells the tale after the Niobe disaster, as the onlookers grow more devout.

scenes.title: Frame: the story is recalled
scenes.summary: The people, awed by Latona's power, recall an older event. One man says he has seen the miraculous pool in Lycia.

scenes.title: The altar in the lake
scenes.summary: The narrator, sent to fetch oxen, finds an ancient altar in a lake with his Lycian guide. The guide explains it is Latona's and tells of her flight from Juno and her birth of the twins on Delos.

scenes.title: Latona begs for water
scenes.summary: Thirsty Latona reaches a lake where rustics gather reeds. She kneels and pleads for water, but they forbid her.
scenes.stakes: Latona and her infants risk dying of thirst and exhaustion.

scenes.title: The rustics become frogs
scenes.summary: The countrymen threaten her and stir up the mud. Latona curses them to live in the pool, and they become croaking frogs.
scenes.stakes: The countrymen risk the goddess's wrath for their cruelty.

alias_notes.explanation: Latona belongs to the Titan generation.

notable_quotes.reason: Latona argues that sun, air and water belong to no one.
Her curse that shapes the transformation.

analysis.text: Cruelty toward a suppliant is punished by a fitting transformation, as the punishment mirrors the crime. It follows Niobe's pride and shows the gods' vengeance on those who slight Latona.
The tale links to Lycian cult of Latona and reflects Greek ideas of hospitality and the duty to help suppliants.

legacy.text: The story of the Lycian peasants became a standard example of divine retribution in later European art and fountain sculpture, notably the Latona Fountain at Versailles.

fun_facts.text: The Latona Fountain at Versailles, built for Louis XIV in the 1670s, depicts this transformation, with peasants turning into frogs.

language_notes.text: "Clowns" here means rustic peasants or boors, not circus performers.
"Thence" means from that place, i.e. Lycia; "choice oxen" are select cattle.
"Be propitious" is a ritual prayer asking the unseen deity to be favorable and kind.
Naiads are nymphs of springs and streams; Faunus is an Italian god of the countryside.
Delos was a floating island until Latona gave birth there; Juno had forbidden every land to shelter her.
The tree of Pallas is the olive; Latona gave birth to Apollo and Diana beside a palm and an olive.
The Chimæra was a fire-breathing monster, part lion, goat and serpent, said in myth to have lived in Lycia. It marks the region and its harsh heat.
Osiers are willow shoots used for weaving baskets; sedge and bulrushes are marsh plants. They show the men are harvesting from the lakeside.
Titaness: Latona (Leto) was daughter of the Titan Cæus, so she is called a Titaness.
Nectar was the drink of the gods; she says plain water would be as precious to her as that.
'Daughter of Cæus' is a patronymic, naming Latona by her father, a Titan.
The repeated 'beneath the water' imitates the endless croaking and shows the abuse continuing even under the surface.

context_notes.text: Latona, beloved by Jove, bore Apollo and Diana. Juno, jealous, persecuted her across the earth.
Lycia is a region in southwest Asia Minor (modern Turkey).
Juno, queen of the gods and Jove's wife, is the "royal" goddess who banished Latona out of jealousy.
Latona, pregnant by Jove, bore Apollo and Diana and was driven from place to place by Juno's jealousy. The children she nurses here are those twins.
Latona appeals to the ancient idea that natural resources like water and air belong to everyone, so refusing them is a moral offence.

literary_notes.text: The speaker's modest caveat about obscure people lends credibility to his eyewitness tale, framing it as a story within a story.
The ash-blackened altar amid quivering reeds creates an eerie, sacred atmosphere that prepares for the miracle.
Juno's spite fails: Latona gives birth "in spite of" her, and the rival's persecution leads to the twins' birth.
Nature is imagined as a giver who has made sun, air and water common property, supporting Latona's argument.
The narrator asks whom such words would not move, highlighting by contrast the rustics' extreme cruelty.
Resentment 'removes' thirst as if it were a physical substitute, showing her shift from suppliant to avenger.
The men's rude quarrelling continues in the form of croaking, so their punishment perpetuates their very fault.
Concrete details of green back, white belly and joined head and neck vividly complete the transformation into frogs.
